skills.trigger: When determining the anatomical origin (intrapulmonary vs. extrapulmonary/pleural) of a thoracic mass on lateral chest X-ray or axial CT.
steps: On the lateral chest X-ray, assess the anteroposterior position of the mass relative to the spine and sternum; posterior masses often project over the lower thoracic spine and may obscure the posterior costophrenic angle or hemidiaphragm.

On axial CT, evaluate the interface between the mass and the chest wall versus the lung parenchyma; look for an 'extrapleural sign' where the mass displaces extrapleural fat inward or forms obtuse angles with the chest wall.
Distinguish pleural-based lesions from pulmonary ones by confirming the mass arises from or broadly abuts the pleura/chest wall rather than being surrounded by aerated lung tissue.

skills.trigger: When analyzing the association between a thoracic mass and adjacent fluid collections to infer etiology.
steps: Identify the presence of pleural effusion on both lateral X-ray (posterior layering opacity) and axial CT (dependent fluid density).
Assess the spatial relationship: determine if the mass is contiguous with the fluid collection or separated by normal lung/pleura.

Correlate a posterior mass associated with ipsilateral effusion as suggestive of an extrapulmonary/pleural origin, distinguishing it from anterior masses or those without effusion which may suggest different pathologies.
